meta.titre: Bouncer — one notch, one app at a time
meta.description: Bouncer decides which notch app you see on your MacBook. They all stay open, only one shows, and you switch with a two-finger swipe.

chrome.piedLigne: Bouncer, a utility for macOS 14 and later.

heros.chapo: Your notch apps all stay open. Bouncer decides which one you see, and you change your mind with a two-finger swipe.
heros.legendeAvant: Two apps draw in the same place.
heros.legendeApres: Bouncer leaves one of them on stage.

probleme.para1: Vibe Island, boringNotch, Alcove, Notchy: each one draws its own pill under your MacBook’s notch. Open two and they land on the same rectangle, one over the other.
probleme.para2: There is no coordination API, and no such thing as an “active notch app”. <fort>The only way out macOS gives you is to quit one app to use the other</fort>, then launch it again when you need it back.

geste.chapo: Swipe left or right. The next app takes the spot; the previous one stays open and keeps running.

fleches.chapo: If you’d rather use the mouse, bring the pointer near the notch: two arrows light up on either side of the camera housing. When you’re not hovering, Bouncer covers nothing.
fleches.corps: The rest lives in the menu bar: the apps it found, the one on stage, and the settings. Bouncer has no Dock icon and no window to manage.

compatibilite.chapo: And that isn’t up to Bouncer. Better to know before you install.
compatibilite.legendeTableau: Compatibility of the notch apps tested

vibeIsland.note: Measured live, hiding confirmed by recounting the windows.

boringNotch.note: Measured live: the order to hide is accepted and changes nothing on screen.

alcove.note: Verdict read from the binary, not confirmed end to end.

notchy.note: Verdict read from the binary, not confirmed end to end.

compatibilite.para1: The dividing line shows in the binary. An app that leaves its windows in your Space responds when Bouncer hides them. An app that pins them to a private Space it creates itself is outside the standard macOS path: nothing dislodges it without a private API, and Bouncer won’t use one.
compatibilite.para2: Bouncer tests each app once, when it finds it. It marks the ones that don’t respond as “unsupported”, drops them from the cycle, and never tests them again.
compatibilite.para3: Today, out of the four apps tested, <fort>only one takes direction</fort>. The cycle between two apps is written and works, but with no second candidate it has never been verified in real conditions. Check yours with the command in the <lien>README</lien>.

installation.chapo: macOS 14 Sonoma or later, on a MacBook with a notch.
installation.sousLaCommande: Bouncer installs into Applications and opens normally.
installation.archive3: Drag Bouncer into your Applications folder.
installation.citationGatekeeper: “macOS cannot verify that Bouncer is free of malware.”
installation.expliqueGatekeeper: That’s what you’ll see on first launch, and it’s expected. macOS doesn’t know who wrote Bouncer: Apple charges developers $99 a year for an identity it recognizes on sight, and Bouncer doesn’t pay it. The block is about that missing identity, not about what’s inside the app: it is neither damaged nor infected.
installation.gatekeeper1: Double-click Bouncer and let macOS refuse.
installation.gatekeeper2: Open System Settings, then Privacy & Security.
installation.gatekeeper3: Scroll down to the message about Bouncer and click “Open Anyway”.
installation.apres1: Later launches go straight through. With Homebrew you never see this screen, because the cask strips the quarantine attribute itself. That is a Gatekeeper workaround we write ourselves, and it goes away the day Apple notarizes Bouncer.
installation.apres2: Bouncer needs one macOS permission, and only one: Accessibility, which lets it hide other apps’ windows. It asks for it on first launch.
